prompt: A city reports that commuters using a new rail line make fewer car journeys than other residents. It concludes that extending the line will reduce congestion citywide. Which assumption is required?
options: Every resident lives near a station
Rail journeys are always cheaper than car journeys
Congestion occurs only at commuting times
A substantial number of future passengers would otherwise travel by car
explanation: Without displacement of car journeys, more rail use need not reduce road congestion.

prompt: Hospitals introducing an electronic reminder system recorded fewer missed appointments. Which fact most weakens the claim that the reminders caused the improvement?
options: Staff preferred the new system
Those hospitals also began charging for missed appointments
The reminders were sent by text message
Most patients owned mobile phones
explanation: A simultaneous financial penalty is a strong alternative cause.

prompt: A survey finds graduates who studied philosophy report high job satisfaction; therefore studying philosophy makes graduates happier at work. What is the main flaw?
options: Job satisfaction cannot be measured
All philosophy graduates have identical careers
The survey contains too many graduates
Self-selection and career differences may explain the association
explanation: The groups may differ before study or enter different careers, so causation is not established.

prompt: Every proposal approved by committee X was reviewed by a lawyer. Some lawyer-reviewed proposals were rejected. Which conclusion follows?
options: Committee X approved every legal proposal
Approval by X implies legal review
Legal review implies approval by X
No rejected proposal was reviewed
explanation: Only the first statement directly follows from the universal premise.

prompt: A school claims that later start times improved attainment because grades rose after the change. Which finding most strengthens the causal claim?
options: Students said they liked sleeping later
Teachers also preferred the change
The school published the results
Comparable schools with unchanged start times showed no similar rise
explanation: A comparison group without the intervention helps exclude a general trend.

prompt: A policy is justified only if it prevents serious harm and no less restrictive alternative works. Which fact would be most important before applying the policy?
options: Whether similar policies have memorable names
Whether an effective less restrictive measure exists
Whether the policy is popular
Whether it is easy to explain
explanation: The stated principle explicitly requires the absence of an effective less restrictive alternative.

prompt: An online course has a higher completion rate than a classroom course, so moving all teaching online will increase completion. Which assumption is necessary?
options: Online teaching costs less
Every student owns two computers
Classroom teachers dislike technology
Differences in who selected each course do not explain the rate gap
explanation: If the groups self-selected differently, the observed comparison need not predict the effect of moving everyone online.

prompt: A company’s output rose after employees moved to a four-day week. Which evidence most weakens the claim that fewer days caused the rise?
options: The company sells several products
New automated equipment began operating in the same week
Most employees supported the change
Output was measured monthly
explanation: The new equipment could independently explain the productivity increase.

prompt: A columnist argues that because no study has proved a food additive dangerous, it must be completely safe. What is the flaw?
options: The conclusion is too cautious
Studies can never investigate safety
All additives are dangerous
Absence of proof of harm is treated as proof of safety
explanation: Not having established harm does not establish complete safety.

prompt: No efficient process is wasteful. Some automated processes are wasteful. What follows?
options: Some efficient processes are automated
Some automated processes are not efficient
No automated process is efficient
All non-efficient processes are automated
explanation: The wasteful automated processes cannot be efficient, though other automated processes might be.

prompt: A town says protected cycle lanes reduced cyclist injuries. Which evidence best strengthens the claim?
options: Cycling became more popular nationally
The lanes are brightly coloured
Residents remember the construction
Injury rates fell on treated roads but not on similar untreated roads
explanation: A matched untreated comparison makes alternative time trends less plausible.

prompt: Programme A has the higher raw completion rate. Which feature most weakens the claim that A is more effective?
options: Different prior-attainment profiles
Both use percentages
Both have students
The programmes have names
explanation: The groups have different starting profiles, so their unadjusted completion rates are not comparable.

prompt: Students who walk to school have higher average grades. Which most weakens the claim that walking causes higher grades?
options: Walking improves fitness
Students living nearby may have different access to resources
Some students dislike walking
The school promotes sustainable travel
explanation: It supplies a plausible confounding variable related to both travel method and attainment.

prompt: Library loans rose after opening hours were extended, so longer hours necessarily increase reading. What is the main flaw?
options: The sample is too large
The conclusion is too cautious
It does not define a library
It treats correlation as proof of causation
explanation: Other changes could explain the rise, and borrowing is not identical to reading.

prompt: “The city should add cycle lanes because this will reduce traffic.” Which assumption is required?
options: Every resident owns a bicycle
Cycle lanes are free
Some current car journeys would switch to cycling
Traffic is caused only by commuters
explanation: Traffic falls only if some journeys that would be made by car switch mode.

prompt: All debate club members enjoy public speaking. Mira does not enjoy public speaking. What follows?
options: Mira is not a club member
Mira dislikes debating
No member knows Mira
Mira will never join
explanation: By contraposition, Mira is not currently a member.

prompt: A university finds that students attending optional tutorials obtain higher marks and concludes the tutorials are effective. Which consideration most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: The tutorials were taught by experienced staff
Students who choose tutorials may already be more motivated than those who do not
Attendance was recorded electronically
Tutorials covered material that examiners consider important
explanation: It offers a prior difference between the groups that could explain the mark gap without the tutorials helping.

prompt: A council argues that because most surveyed residents support a new road, building it is in the public interest. Which fact most weakens the argument?
options: The road would reduce journey times for most drivers
The survey was conducted over several weeks
A majority of councillors supported the proposal
The survey was sent only to households expected to benefit directly from the road
explanation: A sample drawn only from beneficiaries cannot represent the wider public interest.

prompt: An employer claims a four-day week raised productivity because output per employee increased after its introduction. Which fact is most relevant against the claim?
options: Employees reported preferring the four-day week
The firm’s revenue also increased
The firm installed substantially faster production equipment at the same time
Output per employee is measured over a full year
explanation: It supplies an alternative cause that could account for the whole rise in output.

prompt: A report argues that banning cars from the centre reduced pollution because measurements fell the following month. Which assumption is required?
options: Seasonal weather changes did not account for the measured reduction
The ban was enforced by traffic cameras
Residents were consulted before the ban
Pollution is measured at several sites
explanation: Without this, the fall could be due to weather rather than the ban.

prompt: A school says replacing textbooks with tablets improved learning because students completed homework faster. What is the central flaw?
options: Tablets are more expensive than textbooks
Some students preferred printed textbooks
Faster completion does not by itself show greater learning
The tablets were provided by a technology company
explanation: The evidence measures speed, but the conclusion is about the quality of learning.

prompt: A study finds that people who drink coffee live longer, and concludes that coffee extends life. Which fact most weakens this conclusion?
options: Coffee contains antioxidants
Coffee drinkers tend to be wealthier, and wealthier people live longer
Some people dislike the taste of coffee
The study was published recently
explanation: It identifies a third factor linked to both coffee drinking and longevity, offering an alternative explanation.

prompt: A school bans mobile phones and grades improve, so the ban raised attainment. Which finding most strengthens this claim?
options: A comparable school without a ban saw no change in grades
Students complained about the ban
Phones are popular among teenagers
The ban was announced in assembly
explanation: A control school that did not change supports the ban, rather than other factors, as the cause.

prompt: “The council should ban cars from the High Street because it will reduce accidents.” Which assumption is required by this argument?
options: All residents own cars
The High Street is the busiest road in the city
Cyclists also use the High Street
At least some accidents on the High Street are caused by cars
explanation: The ban can only cut accidents if cars contribute to them in the first place.

prompt: “Everyone I know likes the new policy, so everyone likes it.” What is the main flaw?
options: The conclusion is too modest
The sample is unrepresentative of the whole population
The evidence is irrelevant to the conclusion
It assumes people are honest
explanation: A person’s acquaintances are not a representative sample of everyone.

prompt: All poets read widely. Sam does not read widely. What follows?
options: Sam is not a poet
Sam is a poet
Sam dislikes poetry
Some poets do not read widely
explanation: By contraposition, anyone who does not read widely is not a poet.

prompt: Crime fell after more police were hired, so hiring police reduces crime. Which fact most weakens this argument?
options: Police numbers rose by 10%
The police chief supported the policy
Crime fell nationally over the same period
Some crimes are never reported
explanation: If crime fell everywhere, the local fall may have nothing to do with the extra police.

prompt: “Vitamin C prevents colds, because people who take it get fewer colds.” Which assumption is required?
options: Vitamin C is inexpensive
Colds are caused by viruses
Vitamin C occurs naturally in fruit
People who take vitamin C do not differ systematically in other ways from those who do not
explanation: Without this, the difference could reflect other differences between the two groups.

prompt: “This diet must work because a famous actor endorses it.” What is the main flaw?
options: The evidence is statistical
It relies on a person with no relevant expertise
The conclusion is too weak
The diet is expensive
explanation: An actor’s fame is not evidence about nutrition.

prompt: A trial reports that a drug improves symptoms. Which feature most strengthens the conclusion that the drug caused the improvement?
options: The trial was randomised and double-blind
Participants knew which treatment they received
The drug is expensive to produce
The researchers hope to publish the results
explanation: Randomisation and blinding remove the main sources of bias.

prompt: Some A are B, and all B are C. What follows?
options: All A are C
No A is C
Some A are C
All C are A
explanation: The As that are B must also be C, so at least some A are C.

prompt: Sales rose after an advertising campaign, so the campaign worked. Which fact most weakens this conclusion?
options: The campaign cost a great deal
The product had been redesigned two years earlier
Sales are reported monthly
The main competitor closed during the campaign
explanation: A rival’s closure could explain the rise without the advertising having any effect.

prompt: “This policy is the right one because it is the correct policy to adopt.” What is the main flaw?
options: It appeals to authority
It assumes what it sets out to prove
It uses an unrepresentative sample
It confuses correlation with causation
explanation: The conclusion is simply restated as the reason, so the argument is circular.

prompt: “If we do not act now, it will be too late.” Which assumption is required?
options: Delay makes the problem harder or impossible to solve
The problem is urgent
Everyone agrees there is a problem
Action will be expensive
explanation: The claim only works if waiting genuinely removes the chance to act later.
